I was born in Venezuela, where there's always been a national id card (Cedula de Identidad). I got a unique number assigned to me.

It has many advantages, opening a bank account, getting a loan, all sorts of government interactions are easier when all you have to present is one id. No points system, no problem if your name got misspelt somewhere. In fact, My wife's passport has a slightly different name than her id, no biggie, the id overrides. Need to prove your age? That you are Venezuelan? Going to vote? Bam, just show your id.

I never saw any issue with it, until....

When Venezuelans first tried to recall Chavez, they had to sign the petition and write down their id number. That was the beginning of a form of apartheid, it even had a name The Tascon List, after the guy that compiled it. If you were in that list, you were denied many essential government services (you may be denied a passport or pension, your process would be just stuck forever) just because you had supported the recall, which was our constitutional right.

Which showed me that as inconvenient as it is not to have one, its a worthy price to pay.

Now that I live in a country without id (I'm Australian now), name misspellings across documents are a big problem. Venezuelans tend not to pay that much attention to that since they have the id, so misspellings are somewhat common. Both my wife and brother have had problems because of this
